OK, Juliane. Imagine I’m on the jury, and I know nothing about Brazil. Tell me about your project.
Sure. In Brazil, many people have a credit card, but their credit limit is zero. That was the biggest pain point.
Interesting. I worked at a bank in Boston for five years, and we never had that problem. Why is it so important here?
Our key insight was this: here, a credit card is an extension of the salary. So at first, we talked to many customers.
Good. And then?
Then we built a prototype: a game. The customer completes simple behaviors, like paying bills on time, and earns a limit as a reward.
I love that. When did you launch it?
We launched it inside the app, and since the launch many customers have earned a limit.
That’s your ending. Two years ago I was on a design jury, and I read hundreds of entries. The good ones always finished with a result.
Thanks, Tom. So far, this is the best version of my story.

Hi, I'm Arjun, and I'm a product designer in Mumbai. Let me tell you a short product story. Two years ago, we talked to young customers, and they all had the same pain point: they wanted to save money, but at the end of the month, nothing was left. Our insight was that saving felt like a punishment. So we built a prototype that saved a small amount every time the customer paid with the card, like a game. We tested it with fifty people, and they loved it. We launched it last year. Since the launch, more than two hundred thousand people have used it, and the average savings have doubled. So far, it's my favorite project.

Hello, I'm Giulia, and I'm a designer from Milan. I have been on five design juries, and I have read a lot of product stories. The good ones always have three parts. First, the problem: who had it, and why it mattered. Second, what the team did: the research, the prototype, the tests. Third, the result: what has changed for real people since the launch. One team I remember very well. They didn't show many numbers. They showed a photo of one real customer and told her story, from the problem to the result. I still remember her name. That is what a jury remembers: people, not slides.
